searchText: > (2) There is no definitive TX scoring function in the EIP. It would be nice to define one. This would really simplify the txpool implementation. This feels out of scope for the EIP. It is not something that requires consensus and doesn't need a standard. That being said, I think there may be value in coming up with recommendations for clients that we can share outside the EIP. <@194432762315407360> I thought a new block just involved sending the block header, and then if the node didn't recognize it they would ask for the transaction list (just list of IDs), and then they would request any IDs they didn't have? No, it's not like that For a particular reason, or just because it was easier to send the entire block? Something I find mildly frustrating is that the main argument against 1559 feels like, "the network is currently attackable, and 1559 makes it more attackable. However, if that is the case it feels like our number one priority above all else right now should be solving "the network is attackable", yet we are struggling to get stuff like 2930/2929 through quickly, and I haven't really heard any serious (as in, short term fixes) beyond that yet it sounds like that isn't enough to secure the network against attacks. If 1559 is blocked by the current known vulnerabilities, what can we do to mitigate those vulnerabilities and unblock 1559? Keep in mind, 1559 addresses an *economic* vulnerability (selfish mining attacks), so I feel like it is pretty important in terms of mitigating attacks, though I appreciate that DoS attacks may be more of a threat at the moment. (I should mention that I personally continue to think the fears about short term load skipes are vastly overblown; for example I think if the gas limit temporarily rose to 50m for 5 minutes right now, the worst thing that could happen is that the chain would be unusable for 5-10 minutes) Do we know how to create these attack blocks? Can we integrate those into our EIP-1559 testing to see how bad things get and how expensive such an attack would be? I see no evidence that there's a DoS issue that does anything but lead to blocks taking a long time to process (eg. an out-of-memory bug would do that) I'd definitely support us pushing for 2929 (with or without 2930) What can we do to convince everyone that the worst case scenario isn't so bad? Weren't we supposed to have testnets to do that by now? Perhaps we can put 2929 onto the 1559 testnet to start? How hard would that be <@!574864862338088960> <@!489256758989029405>? Or isn't whiteblock or someone doing experiments with 25m gas blocks? I think we *do* have testnets for that, but I don't think the people operating them know how to construct the attack blocks. Oh that's easy: just have a transaction that contains a list of accounts in the state (or some accounts in the state, some accounts not in the state), and then just do "BALANCE(account1); BALANCE(account2); BALANCE(account3)...." each transaction would need to point to different accounts, so you keep accessing things that are not in the cache <@!574864862338088960> Can we get some tests going where we have ☝️ consuming all gas? Oh, perhaps the hard part is generating enough accounts/state first. This is where it would be *really* useful to be able to fork mainnet. can't you just import mainnet? Like, have a testnet with *exactly* identical rules to mainnet So you can import mainnet blocks Except add a hard fork that resets difficulty at block (now + 1) And then just have miners vote the gaslimit up to 25m Last I checked, none of the clients support that. I think we need to write up an EIP that all clients should implement but have no fork block number defined for mainnet. This EIP would just define a strategy for setting difficulty to epsilon as part of a hard fork. I don't believe this is the first time that someone has wished for the ability to "fork mainnet" via config. ok, so I would say (i) do that, but (ii) just go fork geth to add that HF on your own today > Oh, perhaps the hard part is generating enough accounts/state first. <@!301186049323958275> Yes this is the hard part We did some tests at 38M gas block but with a small state, and with only Besu nodes. So absolutely not comparable to mainnet This is why i said we need people working on that. It is hard for me alone to manage the implementation, the integration testnet and performance testing Geth is still not ready to be included in the testnet. Since this is the major client, this is a blocking issue for performance testing Do you think it would be valuable if we manage to fork mainnet with EIP-1559 enabled Besu + Nethermind nodes ? hmm why is it not ready? implementation not done yet? > Yes. They have consensus issues Oh btw, quick check: is the version of 1559 that's being implemented the simplified single-mempool type? yes, single pool and no transition period ok great > Do you think it would be valuable if we manage to fork mainnet with EIP-1559 enabled Besu + Nethermind nodes ? I'd say yes Because parallelizing work is always good Ok. I will raise that internally and see if we could do that soon. So this way, when geth becomes ready, you'll have a working testnet that you can put geth onto Yes I agree btw another really fun fact is that even if you're skeptical of bursts, EIP 1559 is *definitely* safe enough when we do eth2 😆 The reason is that PoW because of its poisson distribution of block times has a naturally spiky block distribution, and we get a 5-minute-long capacity doubling on average about once a week, but eth2 has blocks cleanly coming once per 12 seconds, so this no longer is a problem And so EIP 1559 just comes in and replaces the bursts that PoW used to already provide <@!273808422753796097> Are the attacks people fear supra-linear? That is, a single block/transaction is worse than 2 blocks or 2 transactions of the same gas? If the attack is linear with gas, then I would want to be convinced that this attack is anything we should worry about since we aren't changing the average block time. I know no evidence of anything super-linear in transaction processing. But if that was the problem, we could just add a per-tx gas cap in 1559? Wait didn't early versions of 1559 already have that? I know that I yelled about the idea a few times way back then Was removed with the consolidation of pools (effectively). We removed it. There was the 8M limit eh, imo we should add it back in (though maybe at 10m or 12.5m now) It's a good stopgap imo Eh, I'm not a fan of adding code just to combat FUD. If someone has a real supra-linear attack they should express/share it with the group. Maybe we should ask the devs explicitly, "are you worried about linear attacks or superlinear attacks?" If not, we shouldn't be spending time/effort/complexity on protecting against made up attack vectors. That is probably a good first step. Maybe <@!552133098075193354> can find the answer for us? They have been good at getting answers. 🙂 TL;DR <@!552133098075193354>: Find out from the people who are worried about attacks against larger blocks whether they are scared of an attack vector that is supra-linear with gas used in a block or gas used in a transaction. If so, are they aware of such an attack vector, or just afraid one might exist? To clarify, the question is, are the attacks people are worried about (i) super-linear wrt gas in a block, (ii) super-linear wrt gas in a transaction or (iii) linear but with high constant factors If we do a EIP-1559 testnet fork of mainnet, we should include 2929 ? If the attacks people are worried about are linear I care far less about testing combined 2929+1559. I think that test is particularly useful if there is a fear of super-linear with gas attacks. Also, I think we would need mainnet fork + 2929 + 1559 on a primary client (Geth, Nethermind, OpenEthereum). Ok > Ok sounds good. Give me your address whenever you want. I will add another Besu validator then. <@!574864862338088960> I've just created an eip1559 validator node and <@!489256758989029405> asked me to provide you an address, so here it is: `0x709a1575d347e5a8fccc23529b6e630ad0650cfb` > <@!574864862338088960> I've just created an eip1559 validator node and <@!489256758989029405> asked me to provide you an address, so here it is: `0x709a1575d347e5a8fccc23529b6e630ad0650cfb` <@!199273991058227200> I added your node as a validator. Also could you please use the eth stats service we provided ? That would be useful. `$NODE_NAME:7pyzQMYIWkrPZ7ab@18.191.65.105:3001` > To clarify, the question is, are the attacks people are worried about (i) super-linear wrt gas in a block, (ii) super-linear wrt gas in a transaction or (iii) linear but with high constant factors My hunch is that the "broken metre"-type attacks are maybe super-linear wrt gas in a block (e.g. if we can create a bad block now that just slows the network down, a 2x bad block may do worse than that, for example crashing the node). I don't see why (ii) would be the case, and no idea on (iii). I'll follow up and try and provide a better answer. FWIW, re: 2929, I don't think anyone really opposes it. I'm also strongly in favor of getting it done ASAP and hope that before London we'll also see good progress on flat-DB approaches across Geth (with snapshot), TurboGeth and Besu. I'm not sure if Nethermind is working on anything in that area cc: <@!489256758989029405> ? yo tim yup, is there some approach from BeSu too? I tested a sample flatdb solution last Saturday for Nethermind and we plan to add it as an option some time nov/dec Nice! Yes, on Besu we're working on something like that. It's still pretty experimental, but we expect to have something to show by end-of-year/early next year. do we plan to have a common format or is everyone trying to build their own thing? 🙂 ? Pretty sure we're all building our own thing 😅. maybe should arrange a call and discuss how we want to have it? I think it could be interesting to have a flat-DB call, yeah. I'd be curious to get a braindump from you guys, Geth, TG cool might be worth more than discussing simpler things I'll add it as an agenda item for ACD tomorrow, and we can see if there is broader interest 👍 cool, yeah, great I'm not aware of any supra-linear attacks, only linear with regards to gas. Not theoretical, but practically feasible attacks. The broken metre attacks won't crash a node. Just more gas == slower 2x more gas == 2x slower Cc <@206016661470314496> > "are you worried about linear attacks or superlinear attacks?" To clarify though... I am _aware_ of linear attacks, but of course one can always worry about superlinear attacks. However, I think we (geth-team) aren't _opposed_ to 1559. But we've had higher prio on 2929 and snapsync protocol+implementation. To be clear, I strongly support us shipping both those things before, and I don't see 1559 being ready to ship on mainnet until that's the case anyways 🙂 With Berlin going out in Q4/Q1, it's hard to imagine a fork with other major features happening before summer 2021, especially given that stuff like Account Abstraction is also "ready" and will probably want to go live around the same time. For anyone else building flatdb solutions, but essentially is a trie-backed node (i.e., anyone but turbogeth), I wouldn't mind having a call about it. We hit quite a few gnarly cornercases and had to solve quite a few problems to get it working properly (not to exclude turbogeth - they're welcome to participate too, but I think the set of challenges differ from their perspective) > do we plan to have a common format or is everyone trying to build their own thing? Peter has a spec for the `snap` protocol. Following that spec puts certain requirements on the format, methinks is better to keep snap sync than simply porting the TurboGeth approach to Geth? is there a comparison between the two?

excerpts.author: timbeiko
excerpts.content:
> To clarify, the question is, are the attacks people are worried about (i) super-linear wrt gas in a block, (ii) super-linear wrt gas in a transaction or (iii) linear but with high constant factors

My hunch is that the "broken metre"-type attacks are maybe super-linear wrt gas in a block (e.g. if we can create a bad block now that just slows the network down, a 2x bad block may do worse than that, for example crashing the node). I don't see why (ii) would be the case, and no idea on (iii). I'll follow up and try and provide a better answer.

> "are you worried about linear attacks or superlinear attacks?"

To clarify though... I am _aware_ of linear attacks, but of course one can always worry about superlinear attacks. However, I think we (geth-team) aren't _opposed_ to 1559. But we've had higher prio on 2929 and snapsync protocol+implementation.
